content: Thuja occidentalis, commonly known as the white cedar tree, is an evergreen coniferous tree belonging to the cypress family, Cupressaceae. It is native to the northeastern United States and southeastern Canada, but it is also widely cultivated as an ornamental plant. Thuja occidentalis is naturally distributed from Manitoba eastward through the Great Lakes region and into areas such as Québec, Vermont, New Hampshire, Maine, Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick, and Nova Scotia. Isolated populations can also be found further south in states like Massachusetts, Connecticut, Ohio, Kentucky, Tennessee, North Carolina, Pennsylvania, Maryland, Virginia, and West Virginia. The species was first formally described by Carolus Linnaeus in 1753, and its binomial name remains unchanged. It is known by various common names, including White Cedar (in the UK), Yellow Cedar, Atlantic White Cedar, Swamp Cedar, Cedrus Lycea, Eastern White Cedar, False White Cedar, Hackmatack, Lebensbaum, Thuia du Canada, Techny Arborvitae, American Arborvitae, or simply Arborvitae, particularly in the horticultural trade in the United States. The name Arbor vitae, which translates to tree of life in Latin, reflects the historical belief in the medicinal properties of its sap, bark, and twigs. Despite its common names, it is not a true cedar and is unrelated to the Australian White Cedar (Melia azedarach). Thuja occidentalis thrives in wet forest environments, particularly in coniferous swamps where larger and faster-growing trees struggle to compete. It can also grow in areas with reduced competition, such as cliffs. Although it is not currently classified as endangered, wild populations face threats in many regions due to high deer populations. Deer are particularly attracted to the tree's soft evergreen foliage during winter, often stripping it rapidly. The largest known specimen of Thuja occidentalis stands 34 meters tall with a trunk diameter of 175 cm and is located on South Manitou Island in Leelanau County, Michigan. Under certain conditions, the tree can live for an exceptionally long time. For example, specimens growing on cliffs, where they are protected from deer and wildfires, have been documented to live over 1,100 years. A dead specimen with over 1,650 growth rings has also been discovered. These ancient trees are often small and stunted due to the challenging growing conditions. One notable example is the Witch Tree, a Thuja occidentalis growing out of a cliff face on Lake Superior in Minnesota, which was described as a mature tree in 1731 and remains alive today. In southern Ontario, cliff-dwelling specimens of Thuja occidentalis are the oldest trees in Eastern North America and Canada, with some exceeding 1,653 years in age. The white cedar tree holds significant cultural and practical importance in traditional Ojibwe culture, where it is honored with the name Nookomis Giizhik, meaning Grandmother Cedar. It is considered a sacred gift to humanity and is featured in sacred legends. The tree is one of the four plants of the Ojibwe medicine wheel, associated with the southern direction. Its foliage is rich in vitamin C and is believed to have been the annedda that cured the scurvy of Jacques Cartier and his crew during the winter of 1535–1536. However, the tree contains a neurotoxic compound called thujone, which can be harmful if consumed internally over prolonged periods or during pregnancy. Thuja occidentalis has numerous practical applications. It is commercially used for rustic fencing, posts, lumber, poles, shingles, and log cabin construction. Its wood is particularly valued for the structural components of birchbark canoes, such as ribs and planking, as well as for wooden canoe planking. The essential oil extracted from the tree has been utilized in products such as cleansers, disinfectants, hair preparations, insecticides, liniments, room sprays, and soft soaps. Historically, the Ojibwa people made soup from the inner bark of the tree's soft twigs, and its twigs were also used to brew teas for relieving constipation and headaches. In the 19th century, Thuja tinctures and ointments were commonly applied externally to treat conditions such as warts, ringworm, and thrush. Injecting the tincture into venereal warts was reported to cause their disappearance. Thuja occidentalis is widely cultivated as an ornamental tree, particularly for use in screens and hedges in gardens, parks, and cemeteries. Over 300 cultivars have been developed, exhibiting significant variation in color, shape, and size. Some of the more popular cultivars include 'Degroot's Spire,' 'Ellwangeriana,' 'Hetz Wintergreen,' 'Lutea,' 'Rheingold,' 'Smaragd' (also known as 'Emerald Green'), 'Techny,' and 'Wareana.' The tree was introduced to Europe as early as 1540. Several cultivars, such as 'Danica,' 'Holmstrup,' 'Rheingold,' and 'Smaragd,' have received the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit.
